hints: Look at the displayed structure of glycolic acid and list the two different oxygen containing functional groups present.
Recall which reagent gives effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$ with acids, which gives an orange precipitate with aldehydes and ketones, and which changes colour when an alcohol is oxidised.
Check whether glycolic acid contains an aldehyde or ketone $\text{C=O}$ that would respond to 2,4-DNPH.
Match each positive observation to the group that causes it, the $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group for acidity and the $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ primary alcohol group for oxidation.
walkthrough:
Spot the two reactive groups in glycolic acid**
You have $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. Think of it as two molecules in one. On the right is a carboxylic acid $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$, which is acidic. On the left is a primary alcohol $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$. There is no aldehyde or ketone $\text{C=O}$ with alkyl groups, only the acid $\text{C=O}$.

Carbonate test for the acid group**
Carboxylic acids are strong enough to react with carbonate: $2\text{RCO}_2\text{H} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCO}_2\text{Na} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. You see brisk effervescence as $\text{CO}_2$ bubbles off. So tick for reaction and the group is $\text{COOH}$.

2,4-DNPH test for aldehydes and ketones**
2,4-DNPH gives an orange-yellow precipitate only with the $\text{C=O}$ of an aldehyde or ketone. A carboxylic acid and an alcohol do not react. Glycolic acid has neither, so you observe no change. That is a cross for no reaction and no functional group to name.

Acidified dichromate test for the alcohol group**
Primary alcohols are oxidised by warm acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$, and the orange $\text{Cr(VI)}$ is reduced to green $\text{Cr(III)}$. The $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ group is oxidised, first to an aldehyde and potentially further. So orange to green, tick for reaction, group is alcohol $\text{-OH}$.

Final answer: $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\text{(aq)}$: effervescence / fizzing, reaction occurs ✓, functional group $\text{COOH}$ / carboxylic acid.
2,4-DNPH: no visible reaction / no precipitate, no reaction ✗.
acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$: orange to green, reaction occurs ✓, functional group $\text{-OH}$ / alcohol.

hints: Recall what adds to the $\text{C=O}$ of $\text{HCHO}$ when $\text{HCN}$ with $\text{NaCN}$ is used, and how the carbon skeleton grows by one carbon.
walkthrough:
Build the cyanohydrin from methanal**
Picture $\text{HCHO}$ with its polar $\text{C=O}$. Cyanide $\text{CN}^-$ attacks the carbonyl carbon, then protonation gives an $\text{-OH}$ on the same carbon. You started with one carbon and you add the $\text{CN}$ carbon, so you get a 2-carbon product: $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$, which is 2-hydroxyethanenitrile.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_2\text{(OH)CN}$ displayed as $\text{H-}\underset{\text{OH}}{\overset{\text{H}}{\text{C}}}\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$

hints: Think about what type of hydrolysis converts a $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ group into a $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group in reaction 2.
walkthrough:
Recognise nitrile to acid hydrolysis**
X contains $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ and the product contains $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. That is the classic acid hydrolysis of a nitrile, which needs aqueous dilute strong acid with heating: $\text{R-CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{RCO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_4^+$. Any common dilute mineral acid works.
Final answer: dilute hydrochloric acid / dilute sulfuric acid / dilute nitric acid (heated, aqueous), accept dilute phosphoric acid

hints: Recall the mechanism name when $\text{Br}_2$ replaces a hydrogen on a saturated alkyl group such as $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ to give $\text{CH}_2\text{BrCO}_2\text{H}$.
walkthrough:
Link Br2 on an alkane like side chain to radicals**
You are swapping an $\text{H}$ on $\text{CH}_3$ for $\text{Br}$ using $\text{Br}_2$. That homolytic breaking of $\text{Br-Br}$ to $\text{Br}^\bullet$ radicals and substitution of $\text{H}$ by $\text{Br}$ is free-radical substitution.

hints: Think about what energy source is needed to split $\text{Br}_2$ into radicals to start reaction 3.
walkthrough:
Provide energy for initiation**
$\text{Br-Br}$ needs to undergo homolysis to $2\text{Br}^\bullet$. That bond breaks with light energy, so you need ultraviolet light or sunlight. Heat alone is not the essential Cambridge condition here.
Final answer: UV light / sunlight

hints: Identify the nucleophile $^{-}\text{OH}$ and the electrophilic carbon of the polar $\text{C-Br}$ bond.
Recall the two curly arrows for SN2, one from the nucleophile to carbon and one from the $\text{C-Br}$ bond to bromine, plus where partial charges belong.
walkthrough:
Set up the nucleophilic attack**
Hydroxide has full lone pairs and a negative charge, so it is attracted to the electron poor carbon. Bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so label $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. Draw a curly arrow starting at a lone pair on $^{-}\text{OH}$ and pointing to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{C-Br}$.

Break the carbon bromine bond**
As the new $\text{C-O}$ bond forms, the $\text{C-Br}$ bonding pair must leave with bromine. Draw a second curly arrow from the middle of the $\text{C-Br}$ bond to the $\text{Br}$ atom, giving $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. This concerted backside attack is the $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ step.

Final answer: Curly arrow from lone pair on $^{-}\text{OH}$ to C of $\text{C-Br}$; $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown; curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to Br to form $\text{Br}^-$

hints: Look at what happens to glyoxylic acid, the aldehyde $\text{-CHO}$ becomes a primary alcohol $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$, and decide if that is oxidation or reduction.
walkthrough:
See hydrogen gain as reduction**
The aldehyde part $\text{O=CH-}$ gains hydrogen to become $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-}$. Gain of hydrogen is reduction, so $\text{NaBH}_4$ donates hydride / hydrogen and is itself oxidised. Its role is reducing agent.
Final answer: reducing agent / reductant

hints: Work out the molecular formulae of glyoxylic acid $\text{OCHCO}_2\text{H}$ and glycolic acid $\text{CH}_2\text{(OH)CO}_2\text{H}$ by counting C, H and O atoms.
Balance the hydrogen atoms using $\text{[H]}$ to represent the reducing agent, remembering $\text{[H]}$ provides hydrogen without adding oxygen.
walkthrough:
Write the two molecular formulae**
Count carefully. Glyoxylic acid $\text{O=CH-C(=O)OH}$ has $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_3$$ and glycolic acid $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)OH}$ has $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$$ Carbon and oxygen are already balanced, hydrogen is short by two on the left.

Balance with [H]**
Each $\text{[H]}$ is one reducing hydrogen atom. You need two extra H atoms on the left: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{[H]} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$$ Check atoms: C 2 to 2, H 2+2=4 to 4, O 3 to 3. Balanced.

hints: Recall the two broad O-H regions for glycolic acid in the 1500 to 4000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ range, one for the acid $\text{O-H}$ and one for the alcohol $\text{O-H}$.
Look at spectrum Y between 2500 and 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and decide which broad absorptions are missing compared with glycolic acid.
walkthrough:
Recall what O-H looks like for glycolic acid**
Glycolic acid has two different $\text{O-H}$ groups. The carboxylic acid $\text{O-H}$ gives a very broad, strong band from about 2500 to 3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ sitting on top of $\text{C-H}$. The alcohol $\text{O-H}$ gives a broad band from about 3200 to 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Both would appear in its spectrum.

Read spectrum Y in that window**
In spectrum Y from 1500 to 4000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ you see sharp $\text{C-H}$ around 2900 to 3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and strong $\text{C=O}$ around 1400 to 1750 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, but you do not see the very broad 2500 to 3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ acid hump, and you do not see a broad 3200 to 3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ alcohol band. The absence of both $\text{O-H}$ bands tells you both $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ and $\text{-OH}$ have reacted away.

Final answer: Spectrum Y lacks the very broad absorption at 2500-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{RCO}_2\text{-H}$ of carboxylic acid, and lacks the broad absorption at 3200-3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{RO-H}$ of alcohol, both of which would be present in glycolic acid.

hints: Use the equation $2\text{CH}_2\text{(OH)CO}_2\text{H} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and the loss of all $\text{O-H}$ in the IR to deduce what functional group must be present in Y.
Think how two molecules each with one $\text{-OH}$ and one $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ can join twice with loss of $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give a ring containing two ester links.
walkthrough:
Work out that Y must be an ester with no O-H**
Two glycolic acids lose $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. That is two condensations between $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ to make ester $\text{-COO-}$ links. The IR confirms no acid $\text{O-H}$ and no alcohol $\text{O-H}$ remain, but $\text{C=O}$ remains, so Y contains ester groups and has formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$.

Close the ring to use up both ends**
If you join two molecules head to tail twice, you get a six-membered ring: $\text{CH}_2$ then $\text{C(=O)}$ then $\text{O}$ then $\text{CH}_2$ then $\text{C(=O)}$ then $\text{O}$ back to the start. Draw a ring with alternating $\text{-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ units. That cyclic diester uses both $\text{OH}$ groups and both $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ groups, exactly matching $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$.
Final answer: Cyclic diester (glycolide): six-membered ring $\text{-O-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-O-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-}$ containing two ester groups, molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$
